description: TheFlightEngineer is a solo team led by Lucca, a Brazilian web developer based in Lisbon, Portugal. Lucca builds web apps with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, PHP and MySQL, and has a strong passion for aviation and space.
summary:
Orbi's Outpost is a free browser game that lets kids aged 7–12 run a base on the Moon or Mars and feel the trade-offs behind real space missions. Each day, players share a small power budget between life support, a radiation shield, a greenhouse, science, repairs and calls to Earth. Every choice has a cost, so saving power today can cost oxygen tomorrow.

The solar storms in the game are real events from NASA's DONKI space weather database, including a live feed for the newest storm, and radiation is measured against real ISS dosimeter data from NASA OSDR RadLab. When a mission fails, a friendly debrief explains the cause and effect and shares a real NASA science finding.

It answers the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge by teaching real engineering constraints through play. It works offline on phones and computers, needs no account, and is available in English and Portuguese.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Orbi's Outpost is a turn-based base-management game. Players choose the Moon's south pole or Mars' Jezero Crater and one of three levels: Cadet (ages 7–8), Explorer (9–10) or Commander (11–12). Each day they split up to six power blocks between life support, shield, greenhouse, science, calling Earth and repairs. Power, oxygen, shield and food are shown as four tanks, with crew health and equipment below. Nothing is free: one life-support block makes 14 oxygen while the crew breathes 12 a day, science earns points but costs oxygen and adds radiation, the shield fades every day, and skipped repairs cause glitches later. Communication delay is part of the game (about 1.3 seconds on the Moon and several minutes on Mars).

REAL NASA DATA

  • 51 real solar events (21 flares, 12 CMEs, 18 solar particle events) from NASA DONKI, 2017–2026, stored in the game for offline play.
  • Real ISS DOSTEL dose-rate data from NASA OSDR RadLab (about 294 µGy per day) defines the game's dose unit, the "ISS-day".
  • 11 real OSDR space-biology studies, 14 Moon and Mars facts from NASA Science pages, and public-domain NASA images.
  • "Today's mission" starts with the newest real solar storm from the last 30 days, fetched live from NASA DONKI (tagged LIVE). If that fails or the player is offline, it uses the archived data and says so (tagged ARCHIVED).
  • Real and simulated events are tagged in the game. Storm doses are game-scaled and documented in the project notes.

IMPACT AND CREATIVITY

Failure teaches: the debrief shows a cause-and-effect chain, a timeline chart, what NASA really does, and a "try again with a hint" option. Replayability comes from seeded missions, a daily challenge, shareable mission codes and a classroom mode. Accessibility features include read-aloud, high contrast, reduced motion, bigger text, keyboard play, and English and Portuguese.

TOOLS

HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript (no framework, no build step, no external CDN), SVG artwork, WebAudio sound effects, a service worker for offline use, and Node.js automated tests (37 passing). Balance was checked with bot players: doing nothing never wins. Hosted for free; a small PHP proxy on the host fetches live NASA DONKI data (the key stays on the server, responses are cached for one hour).

USE OF AI

AI tools (Claude and Claude Code by Anthropic) were used to help write the code, the SVG artwork, the documentation and the presentation. The author, Lucca Martins, directed the project: chose the challenge and the idea, planned the game and its requirements (audience, mechanics, levels, real NASA and CSA data sources, accessibility, languages, offline play), guided and reviewed every design and feature decision, played and tested each version on computer and phone, and published the game on InfinityFree and the code on GitHub.

  • No facts were made up by AI: every fact, space weather event and radiation measurement comes from a real NASA, CSA or published scientific source, linked in the game. Gameplay numbers were tuned for fun and are documented in the project notes.
  • No AI image generators were used: the photos are public-domain NASA images, and the artwork is SVG drawn in code.
  • The AI's work was checked, not just accepted: 37 automated tests check the game rules, the data and the deploy, and a browser check covers accessibility, contrast and phone layout. Anyone can run them (instructions in the README).
